Methods & Meanings

INTERPRETING SLOPE AND y-INTERCEPT OF A LINEAR MODEL

A trend line and its equation provide a linear model that summarizes the association between two variables and enables you to make predictions. The slope of a linear model is the predicted change in the dependent variable (Δy) when the change in the independent variable (Δx) is 1 unit. When describing the slope of a linear model, always acknowledge that you are making a prediction, as opposed to knowing the actual value, by using words like "predict," "expect," or "estimate."

The y-intercept of a linear model is the predicted value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero. In statistical scatter plots, the vertical axis is not always drawn at the origin, so you may need to use the equation of the linear model to determine the y-intercept rather than looking at where the line crosses the vertical axis on the graph.

Also be careful about extrapolating the model too far—that is, making predictions that are far smaller or larger than the data values. Models can be valid within the range of the data, but the farther you go outside this range, the less reliable the predictions become.

When describing a linear association, you can use the slope, whether it is positive or negative, and its interpretation in context, to describe the direction of the association. For example, refer to the scatter plot of data about the weight of a car in thousands of pounds (x) and the fuel efficiency of the car in miles per gallon (y). The linear association is negative. The linear model shown has the equation y = 76 − 7.7x. The slope of −7.7 means that for every change in the weight by 1,000 pounds, the fuel efficiency is predicted to change by −7.7 miles per gallon.
